h: Zebras, fleas in frocks and a giraffe named after a Rothschild
p: Walter Rothschild wasn't your average Victorian gent. He famously trained zebras to pull his carriage and even drove a zebra-drawn carriage to Buckingham Palace to prove it could be done. A giraffe subspecies, Rothschild's giraffe, carries his name, and he was utterly fascinated by cassowaries, those big, prehistoric-looking birds from New Guinea and Australia. Knowing a bit about the man makes walking round his museum twice as fun.
He opened the museum to the public in 1892, and when he died in 1937 he left the whole lot to the nation. That's how it ended up as part of the Natural History Museum.

One of the quirkiest things to hunt down is the collection of dressed fleas: tiny insects kitted out in little costumes, a strange bit of Mexican folk art that kids and adults find equally baffling. Get the magnifying-glass mindset on and see who can spot them first.

Behind the scenes, Tring is a serious scientific site too. It's home to the Natural History Museum's huge bird collection, used by researchers from around the world, so the place isn't just a time capsule. It's still working.

Plan on around one to two hours inside, which is plenty for little legs. After that, the Ashridge Estate is a short drive away for woodland walks, and the Tring Reservoirs along the Grand Union Canal are a brilliant spot for birdwatching and an easy flat amble. College Lake nature reserve, just outside town, is another lovely add-on if you've got wildlife fans in tow.
